newsitem.title: USA: U.S. teen sex down after two decades, study shows.
newsitem.headline: U.S. teen sex down after two decades, study shows.

text.p: The proportion of U.S. teen-agers having sex has dropped for the first time in more than 20 years, health officials said on Thursday.
"We welcome the news that the long-term increase in teen-age sexual activity may finally have stopped," Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala said in a statement.
But she called for further efforts to "change the cultural messages that have been accepted too long" about teen sex.
The survey, based on 1995 data, found that 50 percent of females aged 15 to 19 had had sexual intercourse, a five percent drop from the 1990 survey.
A separate but similar study also found a five percent drop for unmarried males in that age group -- 55 percent had had intercourse compared to 60 percent in 1988.

But among girls who had sex for the first time before age 16, 16 percent of them reported that it had not been voluntary. In comparison, among women who had sex the first time at age 20 or older, three percent said the first time was not consensual.
Teen-age sexual activity has been on the rise for at least 20 years. In 1970, only 29 percent of girls in that age group had had sex.

The findings were part of a larger study, slated for release later in May, on childbearing and family planning carried out by the National Center for Health Statistics. The data on teen-age boys was collected separately in a study sponsored by The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development.

The health statistics study also found that women were more likely to use birth control the first time they had sex. Three out of four used contraception the first time, compared to about 64 percent in surveys in the late 1980s. Much of the increase is due to more condom use, the study found.
Among 18- and 19-year-olds, nine out of 10 reported thay had received formal instruction on sexually-transmitted diseases and AIDS prevention, and on how to say no to sex.

Shalala said the decreasing sexual activity and greater use of contraception may be resonsible for the leveling off and recent decline in the teen-age birth rate. The latest data through June 1996 shows that decline has continued.
However, almost two-thirds of the births to teen-agers were unintended. Among all women, the rate of unintended pregnancy is 31 percent.

Shalala in January announced a National Strategy to Prevent Teen Pregnancy, including a "Girl Power!" campaign to enhance self-esteem and prevent unhealthy behavior among young teens. Shalala announced two new community grant programs at a conference in Los Angeles on Thursday to combat teen pregnancy.
At the White House on Friday, first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton is scheduled to honor 12 organizations or individuals working in communities to lower the teen pregnancy rate.
